frameworks.name: Multi-Career Risk-Benefit Framework
frameworks.definition: A decision framework for evaluating the trade-off between a stable, meaningful secondary job and a higher-revenue primary business, balanced against family and personal fulfillment.

claims.text: Design-build ADU construction work yields 80% gross margin on the design phase and 30% gross margin on the construction phase. At this margin split, a $5 million annual revenue business nets approximately $1.2 million profit annually.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: Design-build ADU business model (residential infill development)
Design phase work
Construction phase work
California (San Diego) market

numbers.axis: gross margin by service line, annual revenue to profit

bounded_by: Assumes 70-30 profit split with business partner
Specific to ADU design-build, not other construction verticals

claims.text: A founder working 10 days per month in a construction business (the caller's firefighter schedule) can accomplish 100% of the operational work during those 10 days, creating key-person risk where no work occurs during the remaining 20 days off.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: Construction/design-build business
Founder working externally 20 days/month (firefighter schedule: 10 days on, 10 days off, repeating)
High-capacity founder (can complete work in limited time)
claims.mechanism: The founder's external job forces work compression into 10-day cycles; high personal productivity during those 10 days creates an illusion of sustainable systems while actually masking founder dependency.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses with staffed delivery (e.g., agencies with dedicated teams)
Specific to high-skill founder work (design, client-facing execution)

claims.text: When a founder's margin target requires adding $1.2M-$1.5M in top-line revenue to cover the loss of an external job paying $168,000 salary, the break-even threshold is roughly 4x the salary amount, accounting for split ownership and tax considerations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business (construction, design-build)
Founder with ~25-30% net margin on revenue
Founder considering leaving stable external employment
Shared ownership (70-30 split)
claims.mechanism: Salary lost ($168K) must be replaced by owner's share of incremental profit; at 25% net margins, incremental revenue of $1.2M-$1.5M generates $300-375K profit; split 70-30, the founder nets $210-262K, exceeding the salary.

numbers.axis: salary replacement via revenue growth in construction business

bounded_by: Assumes stable 25-30% net margins continue (supply constraints may prevent this)
Does not account for tax liability on profits
Assumes no decline in founder productivity after leaving external job

claims.text: A founder working a high-autonomy external job (48-hour fire shifts with low call volume: 3 calls/day in affluent area vs. 20 calls/day in urban departments) can accomplish more work for the external business during work hours than at home, because the external job provides uninterrupted focus time.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: External job with 48-hour shifts
Low call volume (3 calls/day vs. urban 20 calls/day)
High-capacity founder with ownership stake in external business
Family with young children at home
claims.mechanism: Low-demand external work (48-hour shifts with minimal active calls) provides protected focus time and allows the founder to complete business work during the shift. Home is fragmented by parenting duties, reducing focus quality. The external job paradoxically becomes the more productive work environment.
bounded_by: Specific to low-call-volume fire departments (affluent suburban, not urban)
Does not apply to high-demand external jobs or founder without young children

claims.text: A founder may resist leaving a stable external job not for financial reasons but because the external job provides intrinsic meaning (helping people, service orientation) that the primary business (profit-focused construction) does not satisfy.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: Founder with high financial security from primary business (>$600K personal net income)
External job providing identity alignment (firefighter with "servant's heart")
Primary business viewed as transactional (construction for profit)
claims.mechanism: The external job offers meaning and identity that money cannot replace; quitting would eliminate meaning even though financial security is already achieved. The real decision is not financial but existential.
bounded_by: Assumes founder has high financial security already ($600K income)
Does not apply to founders whose primary business already provides meaning

claims.text: A founder citing time constraints and productivity concerns as reasons to stay in an external job may be using rationalization to avoid the existential discomfort of quitting, when the actual barrier is fear or loss of identity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder financially capable of leaving
Founder verbally expressing desire to leave
Founder citing rational reasons (time, productivity, family) as barriers
claims.mechanism: When rational reasons are used to justify staying despite admitted desire to leave and financial capability to do so, the real barrier is emotional or existential, not rational. Rationalization masks the true decision obstacle.
bounded_by: Does not apply if rational reasons are genuinely blocking (e.g., founder has no revenue, business cannot survive handoff)

claims.text: In a construction business constrained by skilled tradesperson availability, the founder is the binding constraint not because of tradesperson scarcity but because the founder has optimized the business to run with all discretionary work done by the founder.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: Construction/design-build business
Founder with high personal skill in design and execution
Founder with limited external work time (10 days/month available)
claims.mechanism: By handling all discretionary work personally, the founder makes tradesmen availability a non-constraint and makes founder time the actual constraint. Solving this requires restructuring delivery to not require founder time, not hiring more tradesmen.
bounded_by: Does not apply if genuinely no tradesperson labor exists (geographic/market shortage)

claims.text: A business partner aged 68 who is the primary technical expert ("padded paper guy") in a construction business creates irreplaceable value that prevents scaling beyond current capacity, and this risk increases as the partner approaches retirement age.
claims.speaker: Anonymous ADU/Design-Build Contractor
conditions: Construction/design-build business
Partner age 68 with specialized technical role
No documented systems or junior technicians trained on partner's methods
Partner has not been replaced in 18+ years by the business
claims.mechanism: Key-person dependency on an aging partner creates forced succession risk; the partner's retirement or health decline will cause capability loss that cannot be instantly replaced by hiring. No amount of founder time solves this without pre-emptive training and documentation.
bounded_by: Assumes no documented systems exist to preserve the partner's knowledge
Assumes no junior technicians have been trained
Assumes partner will eventually retire or become unable to work

examples.text: The caller mentioned that his father was diagnosed with cancer 3 years ago, which prompted the caller to become involved in the construction business to ensure the company did not lose money while the father recovered. At that time, the father had invested $20,000 in a job and the business had accumulated approximately $1 million in liquid assets as a result of that investment and the caller's involvement. This example illustrates how a co-founder's health crisis forces succession and demonstrates the value the founder (the father) contributes.

During his 48-hour fire department shifts at a low-call-volume station (3 calls/day in affluent Rancho Santa Fe, California), the caller completes more work on the construction business than he does during his 20 days off at home. He stated: 'I get all that work done. When I go home, I am there.' This illustrates how a low-demand external job provides more protected focus time than home with young children.

The caller stated: 'I'm a servant. I have a servant's heart. That's what I enjoy doing. It's a selfish endeavor, right? Like I help people because it makes me feel good about myself.' This reflects his intrinsic motivation from firefighting. When asked why he hasn't quit despite financial capability, he said: 'the money's not a thing so the money's gone,' but acknowledged that quitting the fire department and moving 100% into construction would mean 'I've created another job I'm going to have to quit another job that I don't like right.' This illustrates the meaning-based barrier to leaving: the external job provides identity and purpose that profit-focused construction does not.

practices.text: Before leaving a stable external job, calculate the incremental revenue required to replace the salary, accounting for ownership split and business margins, to establish a mathematical break-even threshold.

When considering leaving a primary business bottleneck (founder dependency), evaluate whether the constraint is truly external (tradesperson supply) or self-imposed (founder doing all discretionary work), as the solution differs.

If a business partner is the sole expert in a critical technical function, document their methods, train junior staff, or establish redundancy before the partner reaches retirement age to mitigate succession risk.
